h: What a check covers, and what it doesn’t
x: A check covers who can read which rows in the public schema of a database rebuilt from your migrations, plus exposed keys in your code and git history. It can’t see changes made by hand in the Supabase dashboard that never made it into a migration, it doesn’t test your live app, and it isn’t a penetration test. A clean result means our checks found nothing on that date, not that the app is secure

Before we run a full check, you commit one small file to the repo. It stops anyone from checking an app they don’t control, and it takes about thirty seconds.

A report shows exactly which tables a stranger can read and how. That is useful to the app’s owner and useful to an attacker, so we only run the full check for someone who can change the repo. Committing a file is a simple test of that. It also means we need no GitHub permissions at all. You don’t install anything, sign in with GitHub or hand over a token. We read the public repo like any visitor

h: Your decision and the signed receipt

The report also lists any AI, payment or database keys found in your code or anywhere in its git history . A key deleted in a later commit is still readable by anyone who clones the repo. Rotate first, clean up second. If a key is listed, create a new one at the provider and revoke the old one. Rewriting git history alone doesn’t help: the old key may already have been copied.

The last line of the report records how long the run took and which models were tried. We start with the smallest Claude model and only move to a larger one if the lab proof fails, with a spending cap on every check. In our lab study, 15 of 20 apps needed only the smallest model (n=20, 9 Nov 2026).

If no fix passes the strict proof on its own, the check goes to a person instead of guessing. In the same study, 18 of 20 fixes passed the lab proof with no human and 2 went to a person (n=20, 9 Nov 2026). You’ll get an email when the reviewed fix is ready; nothing changes in your repo meanwhile.

h: What a report can’t tell you
x: The lab is only as complete as the migrations in your repo. Policies or tables created by hand in the Supabase dashboard, and never saved as a migration, are invisible to us. We test read access to tables in the public schema, not every query your app makes, and a report is not a penetration test. If something looks wrong, email the founder with the check link.

h: What the badge means, and doesn’t
x: “No known leaks” means our latest check, on the date shown, found no personal data readable by the wrong people in the tables we test. It isn’t a certificate or a guarantee about the whole app. Tables your team marked as intended still count today, so an app with only intended public tables shows “fix in progress”.
Every finished check comes with a receipt signed with Ed25519. Anyone can confirm it came from PatchLabs and hasn’t been edited since: a client, an investor, an auditor, or you in a year’s time.

A receipt is issued for every check that finishes as done , no_leaks or needs_review . It records: check_id , repo Which check, of which repo. status The result: done , no_leaks or needs_review . tables_leaking Every table the check found readable by the wrong people. lab_proof_passed Whether the fix passed all three tests: anonymous visitor denied, stranger denied, owner still reads their own row

h: Check a fix file against its receipt
x: fix_sha256 is the SHA-256 of the fix exactly as we served it. Hash the downloaded file and compare: Terminal Copy shasum -a 256 20261109165600_patchlabs_leak_fix.sql # or: sha256sum … A match means the migration you are about to apply is byte for byte the one the lab proved. An editor that adds a trailing newline will change the hash, so compare the file as downloaded.

If we ever replace the signing key, receipts signed with the old key will no longer verify against the published one (their key_id won’t match). We will announce any change on the changelog , with the retired public key.

A receipt proves that PatchLabs issued these results for this check and that nobody has edited them since. It doesn’t re-run the lab, and it says nothing about commits made after finished_at . For the current state of an app, run a re-check.

A recorded approve or reject on a finished check, with who, when and why. Included in the signed receipt.
The branch GitHub shows first, usually main . Verification and every check read this branch.
What changed between an app’s last two checks: new leaks, fixed, still leaking, and marked as intended.
A widely used digital signature scheme. We sign receipts with it so anyone can check them against our published public key.
A stable code for a kind of problem the free RLS check spots, from PL-001 (anyone with the public key can read personal data) to PL-008 (row level security not enabled). The list .
A SQL migration (plus any code change it notes) that closes a leak. Called a proven fix once it passes the lab proof.
The part of a check that looks for exposed AI, payment and database keys in your code and its full git history.

A disposable local Postgres that copies Supabase’s roles, auth functions and default grants. We rebuild your database in it from your migrations, test it, and throw it away. It never touches your live app.
The three tests a fix must pass: anonymous visitor denied, signed-in stranger denied, owner still reads their own rows.
Personal data that the wrong people can read: an anonymous visitor, or a signed-in user who doesn’t own it.
Model Context Protocol: a standard way for AI coding agents to use outside tools. PatchLabs runs a remote MCP server. More .
A SQL file in supabase/migrations/ that changes your database’s structure or rules. Migrations run in filename order, which is why fix files start with a timestamp.
A check status meaning leaks were found but no fix passed the proof on its own, so a person reviews it before you apply anything.
The test user who owns a seeded row. After a fix they must still read their own data, or the proof fails.
The role that manages a workspace: invites, roles, webhook and name. The other role is member. More .
Information about a person, such as an email address, phone number, home address or date of birth. These are the columns a check looks for.
A row level security rule in Postgres that says who may read or change which rows, for example “users can read their own profile”.
A fix that has passed the lab proof . A scanner gives you a finding; a proven fix is one you’ve seen work.
Another check of the same app, on a schedule, from Run now, CI or MCP. The quickest way to confirm a fix is live.
A signed record of a finished check: result, tables, whether the proof passed, the fix’s hash, and every decision and answer. More .
A decision that says “these tables are meant to be readable”. Creates a suppression .
The Postgres feature Supabase uses to decide which rows each user can see. When it’s off, or a policy is too broad, data leaks.
Fake rows we put in the lab database so there is something to read. Never real data.
A Postgres function that runs with its creator’s rights instead of the caller’s. Useful, but risky if anyone can call it or its search_path isn’t fixed.
Supabase’s secret key that bypasses every policy. It must never appear in frontend code or a repo; the key scan looks for it.
In the lab, a freshly signed-up user who owns nothing. If they can read other people’s rows, anyone who signs up can.
A table your team marked as intended for one app. Later checks list it as “marked as intended” and don’t alert on it. More .
patchlabs-verify.txt , committed with a one-time code to prove you control the repo. More .
A URL we POST to when a check finishes. Works with Slack and Discord incoming webhooks. More .
Where apps, members, API keys, the webhook and the plan live. You can belong to several. More .
